content: Clinical engineering is a specialized field that focuses on the application of engineering principles and technology to enhance and deliver healthcare services. While its origins can be traced back to the 1940s, the term clinical engineering was first introduced in 1969. Over time, the field has evolved from an initial emphasis on research activities to a primary focus on the maintenance of medical equipment. Efforts have been made to expand the scope of clinical engineering to include activities such as pre-purchase equipment evaluation, incident investigation, equipment management, productivity analysis, cost-effectiveness studies, integration of information systems, and patient safety initiatives. However, these attempts have achieved only limited success. The history of applying engineering to medicine spans decades or even centuries, depending on the perspective. For instance, Stephen Hales' work in the early 1700s, which led to the invention of a ventilator and the discovery of blood pressure, clearly involved the application of engineering techniques to medicine. The first modern professional intersociety engineering meeting focused on the application of engineering in medicine likely occurred in 1948, as noted by the Alliance for Engineering in Medicine and Biology. The term clinical engineering was explicitly mentioned for the first time in a 1969 paper by Landoll and Caceres. Dr. Cesar A. Caceres, a cardiologist, is widely credited with coining the term clinical engineering. In the early 1970s, clinical engineering was anticipated to become a field requiring a significant number of professionals. However, at that time, only 300 to 400 clinical engineers were employed in hospitals. Subsequent decades have shown no substantial growth in the number of clinical engineers employed, with some evidence suggesting a decline. For example, the International Certification Commission for Clinical Engineers (ICC) was established in the early 1970s under the sponsorship of the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation (AAMI) to provide formal certification for clinical engineers. A similar certification program was created by academic institutions offering graduate degrees in clinical engineering, known as the American Board of Clinical Engineering (ABCE). In 1979, the ABCE dissolved, and those certified under its program were integrated into the ICC certification program. By 1985, only 350 clinical engineers had achieved certification. In 1999, after extensive deliberation and analysis of a 1998 survey indicating a lack of a viable market for its certification program, AAMI decided to suspend the program and ceased accepting new applicants as of July 1999. A new clinical engineering certification program was launched in 2002 under the sponsorship of the American College of Clinical Engineering (ACCE) and administered by the ACCE Healthcare Technology Foundation. In 2004, the first year of the new certification process, 112 individuals were certified based on their previous ICC certification, and three individuals received new certifications. By the publication of the 2006-2007 ACCE Healthcare Technology Foundation Annual Report, a total of 147 individuals had been certified. A clinical engineer is defined as a professional who supports and advances patient care by applying engineering and managerial skills to healthcare technology. This role often involves interdisciplinary collaboration with physicians, nurses, medical technologists, IT professionals, pharmacists, administrators, medical device manufacturers, and regulatory authorities. Clinical engineers typically work alongside Biomedical Equipment Technicians (BMETs) to support and maintain medical devices used in patient care settings. This definition was first adopted by the ACCE Board of Directors on May 13, 1991. However, two issues remain unresolved in this definition, leading to some confusion. First, the distinction between a clinical engineer and a biomedical engineer is not always clear, as the terms are often used interchangeably. Some hospitals refer to their medical equipment maintenance departments as clinical engineering departments, while others call them biomedical engineering departments. Technicians are almost universally referred to as biomedical equipment technicians, regardless of the department's name. Generally, the term biomedical engineer is considered broader, encompassing engineers involved in the design of medical devices for manufacturers, whereas clinical engineers typically work in hospitals, addressing issues directly related to the use of equipment in patient care settings. The second unresolved issue pertains to the appropriate educational background for a clinical engineer. Certification programs generally expect applicants to hold a bachelor's degree in engineering, although exceptions exist for individuals with sufficient years of engineering practice. As a general rule, most clinical engineers are trained as engineers and possess the academic credentials to demonstrate this. The management of healthcare technology is becoming increasingly complex. The driving factors and opportunities in this evolving field are explored in The Future of Clinical Engineering, published in the IEEE EMBS magazine in 2003.
